debateSummary: WCAG 2.x 4.5:1 contrast math fails in dark mode and modern OLED displays. WCAG 3 explores perceptual contrast (such as APCA), calculating contrast based on spatial frequency, font weight, font size, and polarity.
whyItIsHeated: Designers appreciate that perceptual contrast accounts for visual context, but developers and tooling vendors caution about complexity and backward-compatibility with existing design systems and statutory 4.5:1 benchmarks.
currentWorkingGroupTrajectory: The working group is evaluating perceptual contrast algorithms while considering migration bridges and tooling feasibility before finalizing normative contrast metrics.

topic: 📐 Font Sizing Units: Absolute (px) vs. Relative (rem)
debateSummary: Whether WCAG 3 should anchor text sizing and zoom requirements in CSS px, rem, or visual angle and x-height.
whyItIsHeated: Advocates for rem argue that px overrides user browser preferences for root font size. Working group contributors note that CSS px is defined by visual angle and that browser zoom operates independently of root font units.
currentWorkingGroupTrajectory: Active discussion on separating technology-independent requirements from technology-specific methods, ensuring zoom and text enlargement function reliably across user agents without unduly restricting author units.

links.title: W3C WCAG 3 Issue #642: Replace absolute units (px) with relative units (rem)

debateSummary: To evaluate qualitative requirements (such as plain language, content reviews, and user research), WCAG 3 introduces Assertions—procedural statements where an organization documents its testing and governance.
whyItIsHeated: Proponents argue assertions incentivize authentic usability testing with disabled users. Others express caution that corporate self-reporting must be verifiable with strict evidence criteria to prevent unverified compliance claims.
currentWorkingGroupTrajectory: Under the 6-tier reporting structure, assertions are placed in tiers beyond conformance (Tier 4 Bronze, Tier 5 Silver, Tier 6 Gold), meaning base conformance (Tier 3) is evaluated on core requirements without relying on assertions.

links.title: W3C WCAG 3.0 Editors' Draft: Reporting Tiers

debateSummary: WCAG 2.2 evaluates accessibility as a strict pass/fail checklist per page. The working group has explored whether WCAG 3 should use continuous point-based scoring (0-4 per outcome) or qualitative reporting tiers.
whyItIsHeated: Continuous scoring allows organizations to measure incremental accessibility improvements, but risks allowing high scores on peripheral content to average out severe blockers on essential workflows.
currentWorkingGroupTrajectory: The latest draft establishes reporting tiers based on severity tags (harm, barrier, friction), while keeping an alternative scoring proposal open for public feedback.
w3cStatus: Reporting Tiers Drafted with Alternative Scoring Proposal Open for Comment

debateSummary: WCAG 2.2 permitted non-accessible web pages if a secondary accessible 'text-only' alternate version was provided.
whyItIsHeated: The working group strongly emphasizes native, inclusive accessibility to prevent secondary experiences that often become stale or segregated. Discussions focus on how to handle legitimate media alternatives and responsive views.
currentWorkingGroupTrajectory: Strong consensus to eliminate separate alternate URLs in favor of responsive page variations and native equivalents embedded within the primary product.

links.title: W3C WCAG 3 Discussion #623: Conforming Alternate Versions in WCAG 3
W3C WCAG 3 Issue #682: Page Variations Conformance Requirement

debateSummary: Global accessibility laws (US Section 508, ADA Title II/III, EU EN 301 549, European Accessibility Act) currently anchor compliance to WCAG 2.x Level AA.
whyItIsHeated: Regulators require clear, enforceable baselines. Shifting from Level AA to a single core conformance bar with reporting tiers requires informative guidance so policymakers know which tier to specify in statute.
currentWorkingGroupTrajectory: The working group plans informative guidance for regulators and procurement officials recommending how to utilize reporting tiers (e.g. Tier 3 for base compliance, higher tiers for large entities or public procurement).

links.title: W3C WCAG 3.0 Editors' Draft: Progress Towards and Beyond Conformance

debateSummary: Balancing touch target accessibility on mobile devices with high-density data tables and toolbars on desktop viewports.
whyItIsHeated: Touch users benefit from larger targets (such as 44x44px), while dense enterprise desktop applications struggle to fit large targets without excessive scrolling or altered density.
currentWorkingGroupTrajectory: Provisions distinguish baseline minimum target requirements with spacing offsets from enhanced supplemental target dimensions.

links.title: W3C WCAG 3 Repository: Target Size & Spacing Issues

debateSummary: How to define objective thresholds for flashing and motion triggers to protect users from photosensitive seizures and vestibular disorders.
whyItIsHeated: Defining exact contrast change thresholds, duration, and screen area coverage across diverse screen sizes, zooms, and viewing distances is technically complex.
currentWorkingGroupTrajectory: Provisions restructured under PR #628 into no-flashing-over-threshold and no-flashing-over-threshold-no-exceptions, with exploratory work on single-flash contrast transitions.
w3cStatus: Merged in PR #628, Active Discussion in #629

W3C WCAG 3 Issue #629: Flashing and User Preferences

debateSummary: Ensuring focused elements are not hidden by sticky headers, footers, cookie banners, or floating chat widgets.
whyItIsHeated: Developers need clear guidance on automated detection and responsive layout handling (e.g., using scroll-padding and scroll-margin).
currentWorkingGroupTrajectory: Focus visibility and non-obscuration are recognized as essential for keyboard navigation, transitioning from WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.11/2.4.12 into WCAG 3 navigation provisions.

links.title: W3C WCAG 3 Repository: Focus Obscuration Issues

debateSummary: Whether web content should automatically respond to OS-level user preferences (such as prefers-reduced-motion, prefers-contrast, prefers-color-scheme) or support custom site-level controls.
whyItIsHeated: OS preferences convey user needs directly, but users sometimes require per-site overrides or access settings when using shared devices where system settings cannot be altered.
currentWorkingGroupTrajectory: Guidelines encourage respecting platform media queries by default while allowing user-controllable in-experience adjustments.
